'''''Grevillea johnsonii''''', commonly known as '''Johnson's grevillea''' or '''Johnson's spider flower''', is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Proteaceae]] and is [[endemic]] to New South Wales. It is a shrub with divided, needle-like leaves and red to orange flowers, and grows in rocky places. 

==Description==
''Grevillea johnsonii'' is a shrub that typically grows to a height of {{cvt|2–4.5|m|ft|0}} and has divided, almost [[Pinnation|pinnatisect]] leaves {{cvt|100–250|mm|0}} long in outline. The leaves have between five and ten, erect, linear lobes {{cvt|0.7–1.5|mm|2}} wide. The flowers are arranged in groups of between eight and ten flowers, {{cvt|30–80|mm|1}} long with a silky, red to orange [[perianth]] with soft hairs near the base. The [[gynoecium]] is {{cvt|25–37|mm|1}} long with a conspicuous, stalked, more or less spherical [[Ovary (botany)|ovary]]. The [[Style (botany)|style]] is red to orange with an oblique [[Pollen-presenter|pollen presenter]]. Flowering occurs from September to November and the fruit is a hairy, more or less spherical [[Follicle (fruit)|follicle]] {{cvt|10|mm|1}} in diameter containing one or two seeds.<ref name="RBGS">{{cite web |last1=Makinson |first1=Robert O. |title=''Grevillea johnsonii'' |url=https://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Grevillea~johnsonii |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney |access-date=1 June 2021}}</ref><ref name="RHS">{{cite web |title=''Grevillea johnsonii'' |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/180997/Grevillea-johnsonii/Details |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society |access-date=1 June 2021}}</ref><ref name="Telopea">{{cite journal |last1=McGillivray |first1=Donald J. |title=Australian Proteaceae: New Taxa and Notes |journal=Telopea |date=1975 |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=22–23 |doi=10.7751/telopea19753102|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Cunn.">{{cite journal |last1=Benson |first1=Doug |last2=McDougall |first2=Lyn |title=Ecology of Sydney Plant Species |journal=Cunninghamia |date=2000 |volume=6 |issue=4 |page=1057 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/299412#page/1073/mode/1up |access-date=24 June 2024 }}</ref> The shrub species typically regenerates from soil stored seed.<ref name="Cunn." />

==Taxonomy and naming==
''Grevillea johnsonii'' was first formally described in 1975 by [[Donald McGillivray (botanist)|Donald McGillivray]] in the journal ''[[Telopea (journal)|Telopea]]'' from specimens collected by [[Lawrence Alexander Sidney Johnson|Lawrie Johnson]] near Kerrabee Mountain and the [[Sandy Hollow–Gulgong railway line]].<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Grevillea johnsonii''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/503640 |publisher=APNI|access-date=1 June 2021}}</ref> The [[Binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] (''johnsonii'') honours the collector of the [[Type (biology)|type]] material, "whose perceptive insights into the Australian flora have added considerably to our understanding of many plant families".<ref name="Cunn." /> The genus ''Grevillea'' was named after [[Charles Francis Greville]], a patron of botany and President of the [[Royal Society]].<ref name="ANBG">{{cite web |title=''Grevillea longifolia'' |url=https://www.anbg.gov.au/gnp/gnp5/gre-long.html |publisher=Australian National Botanic Gardens |access-date=1 June 2021}}</ref> Johnson was a taxonomic botanist, Director of the [[Royal Botanic Garden, Sydney]] and also specialised in the family Proteaceae, to which ''Grevillea johnsonii'' belongs. Common names for this species include Johnson's grevillea<ref name="RBGS" /> and Johnson's spider flower.<ref name="RHS" />

==Distribution and habitat==
''Grevillea johnsonii'' is endemic to New South Wales where it grows in rocky places on [[sandstone]].<ref name="RBGS" /><ref name="Cunn. 2">{{cite journal |last1=Bell |first1=Stephen A.J. |title=Notes on the distribution and conservation status of some restricted plant species from sandstone environments of the upper Hunter Valley, New South Wales |journal=Cunninghamia |date=2001 |volume=7 |issue=1 |page=82 |url=https://www.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/getmedia/72b15b75-1b7a-4b1c-a3aa-dce8f1592ad0/Volume-7(1)-2001-Cun7Bel077-88.pdf.aspx |access-date=1 June 2021}}</ref> The [[National Herbarium of New South Wales]] gives its distribution as "chiefly in the [[Goulburn River|Goulburn]] and [[Capertee River]] catchments with a record from the [[Brogo River]] not verified".<ref name="Telopea" /> The [[Australian Native Plants Society]] suggests that the "common garden red and cream form" occurs near the Brogo River, whereas the orange-flowered form "grows naturally in the Goulburn River catchment at Cox's Gap and several other close by areas".<ref name="ANPSA">{{cite journal |last1=Marriott |first1=Neil |title=''Grevillea johnsonii'' - orange-flowered form |journal=Grevillea Study Group Newsletter |date=February 2016 |volume=103 |page=13 |url=http://anpsa.org.au/grevSG/grev103.pdf |access-date=1 June 2021}}</ref> The species grows natively at an altitude of {{cvt|400-700|m|ft}}, where the annual rainfall is {{cvt|600-700|mm|in}}.<ref name="Cunn." />

It is closely related to the ''[[Grevillea longistyla|G. longistyla]]''.<ref name="ANPSA" /> However, differences are evident through the colour of ''G. johnsonii'', ranging from orange to pink in comparison to the orange and red of ''G. longistyla'' orange to red colours.<ref name="anbg.gov.au">Mullins, E. (1974). ''Grevillea longistyla'' - Growing Native Plants. From https://www.anbg.gov.au/gnp/gnp9/grevillea-longistyla.html</ref> Both species were initially listed as forms of ''G. longistyla'', but have since been separated with a specific status.<ref name="anbg.gov.au"/>

==Ecology==
''Grevillea johnsonii'' is known to attract [[honeyeaters]], but they do not negatively impact the growth and establishment of the shrub.<ref name="ANPSA" /> The fungi ''[[Placoasterella baileyi]]'' and ''[[Seimatosporium grevilleae]]'' can cause leaf spot disease in this species.<ref name="Cunn." />

==Conservation status==
In 2001, the total population of ''G. johnsonii'' was estimated to be well over 1,000 plants. The [[ROTAP]] conservation rating of ''G. johnsonii'' is currently 2RCi, meaning the shrub species is rare, based on the low populations of ''G. johnsonii'' in the Goulburn River area.<ref name="Cunn. 2" /> This indicates that the species is inadequately reserved, with restricted distribution of less than 1000 over a range of 100km.<ref name="anpsa.org.au">Australian Native Plants Society (Australia) - Australian Plants at Risk. (2010). From http://anpsa.org.au/coding.html {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151119075210/http://anpsa.org.au/coding.html |date=19 November 2015 }}</ref> Despite the current rating, collections of the species in recent years has resulted in a proposal to downgrade the ROTAP listing from 2RCi to 2RCa,<ref name="Cunn. 2" /> indicating that the species is now adequately reserved with 1000 or more plants in a proclaimed reserve.<ref name="anpsa.org.au"/>

During the [[2019–20 Australian bushfire season|2019–2020 bushfires]] in southern Australia, the Wildlife and Threatened Species Bushfire Recovery Expert Panel released a "Provisional list of plants requiring urgent management intervention", with ''Grevillea johnsonii'' being mentioned as high priority in its conservation and recovery. It emphasised that its "fire-disease interaction" and the "cumulative exposure to high risks" required conservation action to prevent possible extinction.<ref name="environment">{{cite web |title=Provisional list of plants requiring urgent management intervention |url=https://www.environment.gov.au/system/files/pages/289205b6-83c5-480c-9a7d-3fdf3cde2f68/files/summary-list-plants-requiring-urgent-management-intervention.pdf |publisher=Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Water and the Environment}}</ref> However, many native plants, including ''G. johnsonii'' are capable of regenerating after fire from [[Epicormic shoot|epicormic buds]] on the trunks and/or branches, from a basal [[lignotuber]].<ref name="ANPSA" />

==Uses==
===Use in horticulture===
''Grevillea johnsonii'' was introduced into regular cultivation in the 1950s by Australian botanist [[George Althofer]].<ref name="ANPSA" /> The shrub species is regularly grown in Victoria in comparison to NSW, as the summer rain cannot sustain well drained soils during summer rains.<ref name="ANPSA" /> If ''G. johnsonii'' is [[Plant propagation|propagated]] outside, it is most suitable to use semi-hardwood cuttings and use acidic to neutral, well drained soil.<ref name="RHS" /> It is important to propagate the shrub species in an area that does not maintain full sunlight exposure.<ref name="RHS" /> If it is propagated inside, it should be grown under glass in full light, whereby liquid fertiliser must be provided monthly.<ref name="RHS" /> Once established in the garden, the orange-flowered form tolerates a wide temperature range, including frost, and sets large numbers of seeds that germinate readily after soaking in smoked water.<ref name="ANPSA" /> ''Grevillea'' 'Bon Accord', a [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrid]] formed by a cross between ''G. johnsonii'' and ''[[Grevillea wilsonii|G. wilsonii]]'' has been developed. The broad leaves of ''Grevillea johnsonii'' are [[evergreen]].<ref>Roderick, M.L., Berry, S.L., Saunders, A.R. and Noble, I.R., 1999. On the relationship between the composition, morphology and function of leaves. Functional Ecology, 13(5), pp.696-710.</ref> This species is most suited to a sheltered location, however full sunlight also benefits the species. Soil conditions include well drained soil with the species commonly growing in loam or sand.<ref name="RHS" />

''Grevillea johnsonii'' requires little to no pruning, however if it is propagated inside, more frequent pruning is necessary to restrict size.<ref name="RHS" /> Foliage in autumn, winter and spring is primarily green, however summer will flower with red, pink, and orange forms.<ref name="RHS" />

''Grevillea johnsonii'' sometimes does not produce a strong root ball and may require a [[rootstock]] to be [[plant propagation|propagated]] effectively. Other species of the ''Grevillea'' are useful, such as ''[[Grevillea robusta]]''.<ref>Groesbeck, S.J., 1984. Cultural Studies on the Genus ''Grevillea'' in Hawaii (Doctoral dissertation).</ref>

A notable hybrid of ''G. johnsonii'' is [[List of Grevillea cultivars|''Grevillea'' 'Bon Accord']], a hybrid between ''G. johnsonii'' and ''[[Grevillea wilsonii]]''. The hybrid arose in Victoria in 1982, and was registered in 1985 with the [[Australian Cultivar Registration Authority]].<ref name="ACRA">{{cite web |title=''Grevillea'' 'Bon Accord' |url=https://www.anbg.gov.au/acra/descriptions/acc373.html |publisher=Australian National Botanic Gardens |access-date=1 June 2021}}</ref>

===Use in floristry===
The [[vase life]] of ''G. johnsonii'' flowers is limited because the flowers fade and drop their petals rather quickly.<ref>Joyce, D.C., Beal, P. and Shorter, A.J., 1996. Vase life characteristics of selected ''Grevillea''. Australian Journal of Experimental Agriculture, 36(3), pp.379-382.</ref>
